name: Social media detox

image.caption: A 16th century Turkish bath, or #hammam as they call it, in #Sofia #bulgaria at night. #photooftheday 99. One more photo. Then a social media detox!

lead: A social media detox is a set period of reduced or stopped use of platforms. People take one to see fewer idealised faces and bodies, so there is less appearance comparison and a better self-image.

Experiments link viewing idealised images on social networks with higher body dissatisfaction, which is the reasoning behind the break. Meta-analyses of randomised trials report small and sometimes inconsistent effects on well-being; a 2024 meta-analysis found reduced depression but no significant effect on well-being, life satisfaction or stress, and a 2025 study in Body Image compared detox strategies for body image and well-being.

paras: People limit or abstain from apps for days to weeks, sometimes using blocking tools or app timers, or delete apps from their phone. Researchers measure well-being, depression, body image and problematic use before and after. Some people return with a trimmed, more selective feed.
No physical risks. Some people report increased fear of missing out or social pressure during a detox, and results across studies are mixed.

web.title: Social media and body image - Wikipedia

angle.text: A break from social platforms cuts exposure to idealised faces and bodies, which means less appearance comparison and a better self-image. Trials show small, mixed effects on well-being, and appearance outcomes are not directly studied.

lead: A social media detox, a form of digital detox, is a deliberate break from social media or other devices, ranging from usage limits to complete abstinence for a set period.[1]

Research is mixed. Wikipedia summarises a 2024 meta-analysis that found reduced depression but no significant effect on well-being, life satisfaction or stress, and other meta-analyses reporting small improvements in well-being.[1] A 2025 meta-analysis of randomised trials examined detox and well-being,[2] and a 2025 study in Body Image compared detox strategies for body image and well-being.[3]
Sources note that exposure to idealised images is linked with body dissatisfaction in experiments,[4] which is why detoxes appear in appearance-related self-improvement discussion.

paras: Approaches include full abstinence, time limits and app blockers.[1] A survey study examined users' perceptions of detox apps in relation to personality traits.[5]

Meta-analytic findings are small and inconsistent across reviews.[1][6][2] Wikipedia notes critics argue social media provides social capital and that moderation may be preferable to abstinence.[1] A study of relapse predictors examined why people return to use.[7]

A systematic review and meta-analysis examined digital detox interventions and mental health outcomes.[6] A 2025 meta-analysis of randomised trials examined detox and well-being.[2] An exploratory two-week detox study in young adults measured problematic smartphone and social media use and related health outcomes.[8] A 2025 trial reported on in Body Image compared detox approaches for body image and well-being.[3] Experimental reviews on idealised social media images and body dissatisfaction are summarised by Wikipedia.[4]
